A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on influencing human preferences for RLHF. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching results moved between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports three human-subject experiments, analyses of collected preferences, reward-learning evaluations, and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds cross-domain training, stochastic-environment experiments, and participant-survey analyses.

M1.justification: The three intervention mechanisms and original deterministic procedures remain. v3 adds a QUESTION variant targeting change-in-expected-return in stochastic environments, using the new question 'Which path do you prefer to start with?' and the corresponding reward-learning likelihood. This is a limited adaptation rather than a replacement of the intervention framework.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates interventions within the deterministic delivery domain. v3 adds transfer from delivery-domain training to preference elicitation in a space domain with different rewards, and a delivery environment with stochastic tunnel transitions. These test cross-domain generalization and decisions with uncertain outcomes, substantially expanding scenario coverage.

E2.justification: The added stochastic study evaluates change-in-expected-return alongside regret, expanding the compared preference/reward-learning models beyond v1's partial-return/regret pairing. Comparator membership in the original studies is retained: full comparisons removed from the main plots remain in v3 Appendix K.4.

E3.justification: v3 adds separate training and elicitation domains and a stochastic evaluation, each with 10 subjects per condition. Section 5.1 changes normalized return from (Vpi - VU)/V* to (Vpi - VU)/(V* - VU). Reported PRIVILEGED counts change from 64/65/50 to 39/43/42 for partial return/regret/control, but appendix collection totals and subsampling remain unchanged; this does not establish an actual dataset reduction or rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds generalization tests under domain and transition changes, cognitive-load survey analyses explaining unsuccessful regret transfer (Appendix E.3), and analysis of unintended preference-model influence (Appendix I). The synthetic-preference identifiability experiment was already present in v1 Appendix J.6 and is retained in v3 Appendix K.6.

E5.justification: The ten partition seeds and original statistical analyses are retained. Whether accuracy testing changes is unresolved: v3 Table 1 specifies Wilcoxon tests outside PRIVILEGED, whereas Appendix J still specifies Fisher's exact test and retains earlier p-values. The table also marks transfer accuracy as p < 0.01, while Appendix J reports p = 0.049.

E6.justification: Substantial new results accompany the added studies. Transfer accuracy is 86.29% versus 60.0% for partial return and 72.58% versus 72.92% for regret, comparing intervention with control (Table 7). Stochastic-study accuracies are 69.4% versus 67.8% for change-in-expected-return and 61.2% versus 65.9% for regret (Table 9). Original accuracy tables and full learning curves remain unchanged. v3 Figure 13 also corrects v1 Figure 9's significance caption to partial return, p < 0.05.

T1.justification: v1 presents regret through a deterministic-transition derivation. v3 defines general regret using the sum of V* - Q*, separately defines change-in-expected-return and its preference distribution, and distinguishes these models under stochastic transitions (Section 3.2 and Figure 2). This substantially extends the formal framework, although it adds no theorem or proof. The normalized-return definition is also corrected.

C1.justification: The central interface-influence contribution remains, but v3 expands its main claims to three preference models and cross-domain/stochastic settings. The introduction explicitly focuses applicability on sequential decisions, distinguishing single-step LLM RLHF. Introduction and conclusion add model-dependent transfer failures and unintended influence, qualifying the earlier practical-success narrative.

C2.justification: v3 introduces cognitive load and limited remaining improvement over control as explanations for unsuccessful regret transfer. It discusses intuitive rather than explicit computation, unintended influence toward regret, and environment-dependent benefits of question wording. These add substantive mechanisms and applicability boundaries; the earlier partial-return identifiability explanation remains.

D1.justification: v3 documents the space-domain rewards, transfer procedure, tunnel dynamics, and additional survey questions. Conversely, it removes v1 Appendix J.4's hardware specifications and PyTorch/scikit-learn versions. Existing learning hyperparameters, partition seeds, and the shared code/data access link remain.

R1.justification: New Section 2.2 substantially broadens positioning around preference measurement, survey design, annotator discretion, and normative aggregation, citing works including Treiman, Buyl, and D'Alonzo. Section 3.2 also relates change-in-expected-return to Marklund and Van Roy's bootstrapped-return model. This exceeds a limited citation update.

P1.justification: The introduction and conclusion are substantially expanded and rewritten around sequential decisions, transfer, and conditional effectiveness. Related work becomes two subsections, the experimental narrative gains nested follow-up studies, and the appendices are reorganized. The standalone practicality appendix disappears as cross-domain applicability receives direct experimental treatment.

P2.justification: v3 adds an experiment-summary table, new task illustrations, learning and likelihood plots, and accuracy tables. Figure 2 becomes a deterministic/stochastic comparison. Main reward-learning plots are simplified to target-versus-control displays, while the original full comparisons move to Appendix K.4. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v3 directly tests the cross-domain practicality question left as future work in v1 Appendix A, revealing both successful transfer and an important failure boundary. The stochastic study further tests whether interventions distinguish outcomes from decision quality. These additions substantially strengthen assessment of applicability, supported by clearer scope and corrected reporting. Conflicting participant counts and summary-table statistics, an overbroad claim that all training interventions improve reward learning, and removed hardware/software details remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the stronger empirical examination.
